Senses.Note: The former predicate/adjective targets were grammatical uses of the same completeness word and are merged. The Chan deployment includes both lack-nothing formulas and the corpus's criticism of resting on such formulas. The full-precepts compound remains under the precepts gate and should receive longest-match priority when indexed separately. Comparison families include fully endowed from the beginning, completely formed, lack, full precepts, receiving precepts, and precept. Senses.Explanation: To be complete, fully endowed, or lacking nothing. Xuansha says, “each person is fully endowed; each person is manifest” (人人具足，人人成現). Another address ranges across monastics and laypeople, women and men, wise and foolish, noble and low, saying all are fully endowed “without the least lacking” (悉皆具足，曾無欠少). Hongzhi pairs “fully endowed from the beginning” (本來具足) with “not a hair's breadth lacking, not a hair's breadth in excess.” A later text warns that merely accepting “fully endowed from the beginning, no need to seek outside” can become empty talk. In the ordination compound “full precepts” (具足戒), the same completeness word modifies the precepts: biographies record receiving or being given the full precepts. Predicate and attributive placement express the same completeness, not different lexical referents.
